Appendix C Theoretical Background: A Brief Overview of Statistical Learning Theory

C.1 Non Asymptotic Large Deviation Bounds from the 60s: Hoeffding, Bennet, Bernstein

Large deviation bounds refer to bounds on the difference between an expectation and an empirical average. They exist independently of machine learning (contrary to overfitting bounds, below) and are used for polls, Monte Carlo integration, and others.

Indeed, for a dataset size ss, consider δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon} the risk against the randomness ωD\omega_{D} w.r.t. dataset DD of an ϵ\epsilon-divergence between the empirical risk and the risk in generalization for a given parametrization xx, i.e.,

∀(x,ϵ,s),PωD​(|L^​(x)−L⁡(x)|>ϵ)≤δ1,ϵ.\forall(x,\epsilon,s),P_{\omega_{D}}\left(|\hat{L}(x)-L(x)|>\epsilon\right)\leq\delta_{1,\epsilon}. (A.1)

δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon} refers here to the risk of deviation ϵ\epsilon for one (hence the subscript 1) model: when L^\hat{L} is computed by average on a sample, we can invoke δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon} by Hoeffding, Chernoff or Bernstein bounds [Devroye et al., 1996]. By Hoeffding’s bound  [Hoeffding, 1963], if individual losses are in [0,1][0,1] we get

δ1,ϵ=2​exp⁡(−2​s​ϵ2).\delta_{1,\epsilon}=2\exp(-2s\epsilon^{2}). (A.2)

In case we have a prior on a bound σ2\sigma^{2} on the variance of a randomly drawn individual loss, we can use the bound of Bennet and Bernstein [Bennett, 1962]:

δ1,ϵ=2​exp⁡(−s​ϵ​h1​(ϵσ2)).\delta_{1,\epsilon}=2\exp\left(-s\epsilon h_{1}\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\right).

where h1​(λ)=(1+1λ)​ln⁡(1+λ)−1h_{1}(\lambda)=(1+\frac{1}{\lambda})\ln(1+\lambda)-1.

C.2 Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Learning: A Brief Overview

We propose a point of view on optimization algorithms based on their risk of overfitting in the context of huge VC-dimensions and covering numbers, deriving bounds that are not covered by the studies on the rates of convergence. These bounds were frequently developed in the ’90s or ’00s:

  • •

    Sec. C.2.1 presents the Bonferroni correction: whereas “non-uniform” large deviation inequalities estimate the difference between an empirical error and a generalization error for a single predefined classifier (for example when testing a single model on a test set), the Bonferroni correction provides bounds applicable uniformly on a finite set of classifiers (e.g., for selecting, with a validation set, a classifier in a list of classifiers obtained on the training set).

  • •

    Sec. C.2.2 generalizes the Bonferroni correction to infinite families of classifiers: VC-dimension bounds, and others, are the most well-known bounds. They are based on limiting the “capacity” of a space of function, even when it is infinite.

  • •

    Sec. C.2.3 presents other bounds for infinite families of functions, taking into account the optimization algorithm used for selecting a classifier: the idea is that even if the space of functions is large, we can get bounds if the optimization algorithm satisfies some stability assumptions. This last part of the state-of-the-art is the closest to our work: we get non-trivial bounds on deep learning models, independently of the possibly huge number of parameters.

C.2.1 Bounds on the Generalization Loss based on Bonferroni

The Bonferroni bound Bonferroni [1936a], Dunn [1961] is a direct application to statistics of the union bound:

P⁡(A1​ or ​A2​ or …or​Ak)≤∑i=1kP⁡(Ai)P(A_{1}\mbox{ or }A_{2}\mbox{ or \ldots or}A_{k})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(A_{i}) (A.3)

The analysis below extends Videau et al. [2024a], Videau et al. [2024c], using the branching factor analysis in Fournier and Teytaud [2011]. LF​(x)L_{F}(x) refers to the error in generalization for a probability distribution FF and a model xx. L^D​(x)\hat{L}_{D}(x) (frequently denoted L^​(x)\hat{L}(x) in the literature) refers to the random variable corresponding to the empirical error on a dataset DD, of cardinality ss, randomly independently drawn from FF. Whereas gradient-based optimization does not lead to any bound on the generalization loss, such bounds can be obtained when using comparison-based optimization (i.e., a subset of black-box optimization), as detailed below. These bounds suggest that the risk of overfitting is lower than for gradient-based methods. Our experimental results suggest that this interpretation is correct.

Let us see the generalization of large deviation inequalities seen in Sec. C.1.

If we use the empirical error for picking up the best x^\widehat{x}, in a list of bb models x1,…,xbx_{1},\dots,x_{b} (e.g., x1,…,xbx_{1},\dots,x_{b} are chosen by random search or low-discrepancy search or choice by the user, which leads to N⁡(ω,a,b)=bN(\omega,a,b)=b), the risk of deviation ϵ\epsilon for that x^\widehat{x} is at most b⋅δ1,ϵb\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon} (union bound, also known as Bonferroni correction Bonferroni [1936b]) instead of δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon}: Pωd​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|>ϵ)≤δϵ=b​δ1,ϵ.P_{\omega_{d}}(|\hat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|>\epsilon)\leq\delta_{\epsilon}=b\delta_{1,\epsilon}.

Thm 1 extends this to more sophisticated cases, with N⁡(ω,a,b)=πi​ki​(ω,a,b)>>bN(\omega,a,b)=\pi_{i}k_{i}(\omega,a,b)>>b (in many cases, exponential in bb e.g. N⁡(ω,a,b)≤2bN(\omega,a,b)\leq 2^{b} and ki≤2k_{i}\leq 2) instead of N⁡(ω,a,b)=bN(\omega,a,b)=b. In spite of being larger, this bound, exponential in bb, is tighter than bounds based on capacity.

C.2.2 Bounds on the Generalization Loss based on Capacity: Statistical Learning Theory from the 90s

Vapnik [1995b] is a pioneering work on bounds on the generalization loss based on VC-dimension. Many other capacity measures have been defined, such as covering numbers van der Vaart and Wellner [1996] and the fat-shattering dimension Kearns and Schapire [1990]. The most classical bound on the generalization loss is probably the VC-bound in the case of classification:

𝔼⁡[L⁡(x^)]≤infxL⁡(x)+16​V​C​log⁡(s)+42​s\mathbb{E}[L(\hat{x})]\leq\inf_{x}L(x)+16\sqrt{\frac{VC\log(s)+4}{2s}}

(assuming that x^\hat{x} minimizes L^​(x^)\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})). When using shattering coefficients instead of VC-dimension, one can read:

𝔼⁡[L⁡(x^)]≤infxL⁡(x)+16​log⁡(8​e×S​h​a​t​t​e​r​i​n​g​(n))2​s.\mathbb{E}[L(\hat{x})]\leq\inf_{x}L(x)+16\sqrt{\frac{\log(8e\times Shattering(n))}{2s}}.

When it is possible to reach zero loss, then we get

P(L(x^)>ϵ)≤2×Shattering(2n)2−sϵ/2.P(L(\hat{x})>\epsilon)\leq 2\times Shattering(2n)2^{-s\epsilon/2}.

Both the Shattering coefficients and the VC-dimension depend on the class of functions. Extensions exist for regression and other cases, and other capacity measures exist. However, capacity bounds are not always relevant for vast models such as deep networks.

C.2.3 Algorithmic Stability: Bounds based on Properties of Algorithms in the 2000s

Algorithmic Stability [Bousquet and Elisseeff, 2000] is a radically different approach, based on some algorithm properties rather than on the capacity of the underlying family of functions. Because we also use particularities of the learning algorithm to derive generalization bounds, our approach is close to that of Algorithmic Stability.

Following [Bousquet and Elisseeff, 2000], we write l⁡(x,z)l(x,z) the loss of a model parametrized by xx on an example zz, so that L⁡(x)=𝔼z​l​(x,z)L(x)=\mathbb{E}_{z}l(x,z). An algorithm which outputs a model parametrized by x^​(D)\hat{x}(D) on the training data DD has uniform stability β\beta if supD,z|l⁡(x^​(D),z)−l¬i​(x^​(D),z)|≤β\sup_{D,z}|l(\hat{x}(D),z)-l_{\neg i}(\hat{x}(D),z)|\leq\beta for all ii, where l¬il_{\neg i} is the loss of the model learned from a training set obtained from DD by removing the it​hi^{th} example. An algorithm with uniform stability β\beta and some other technical assumptions (including 0≤l≤10\leq l\leq 1) has the following property:

∀δ>0,P⁡(L⁡(x^​(D))>L^​(x^​(D))+1+12​s​β2​s​δ)<δ.\forall\delta>0,P\left(L(\hat{x}(D))>\hat{L}(\hat{x}(D))+\sqrt{\frac{1+12s\beta}{2s\delta}}\right)<\delta.

Appendix D Black-box Optimization Algorithms

The BBoxER algorithmic framework, as illustrated in fig. 2, embeds an algorithm from the family of block-box optimization algorithms, which we now describe in detail.

D.1 Evolutionary Algorithms

For the reasons given in Sec. 3.2, only Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) have been used in the present work, as they are (at least for those uses in the present document) comparison-based, and hence de facto comply with the finite branching factor condition, which is mandatory for the theoretical results of Sec. 4 to hold. Sec. D.2 discusses this choice, and its possible relaxation, while the current section introduces EAs more thoroughly, and details all the comparison-based algorithms used in the experiments of Sec. 5.

Evolutionary algorithms A. E. Eiben and [2015] are stochastic optimization algorithms that crudely mimic the Darwinian evolution of a “population” of μ\mu “individual” (i.e., points of the search space) based on random variations and “survival of the fittest” selection: the μ\mu “parents” generate λ\lambda “offspring” by random operations; the selection process then retains μ\mu individuals to build the next population; in (μ+λ\mu+\lambda)-EAs, these are the fittest of the μ\mu parents plus the λ\lambda offspring, while (μ,λ\mu,\lambda)-EAs select the best of the λ\lambda offspring only. EAs can search any search space on which random variation operators can be defined. These EAs are comparison-based, i.e., only comparisons of the values of the objective are used (to deterministically choose the best ones). But stochastic selection processes can also be used in general EAs.

When it comes to continuous optimization (the variables are continuous), among the most popular EAs are Evolution Strategies (ESs) Beyer and Schwefel [2002], Differential Evolution (DE) Storn and Price [1997], and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) Kennedy and Eberhart [1995].

Evolution Strategies Rechenberg [1973], Schwefel [1977], Beyer and Schwefel [2002] are specific EAs for continuous optimization, using normal “mutations”, i.e., sampling some Gaussian distribution, generally centered on the parent, to generate the offspring. The issue is then to adjust the variance and the covariance matrix of this normal mutation.

The first adaptive ES uses the so-called “one-fifth success rule” Schumer and Steiglitz [1968], Rechenberg [1973], established by theoretical analyses on simple linear and quadratic objective functions, on which the optimal behavior is reached for a success rate (offspring better than parent) of approximately 0.20.2. This is available in Nevergrad as the (1+1)-ES with 1/5th rule, named in this paper OneFifth, whose pseudo-code is given in Alg. 2-left.

CMA-ES Hansen and Ostermeier [1996], Hansen and Ostermeier [2003], Hansen [2023] iteratively updates a multivariate Gaussian random variable, initialized at the identity and parametrized by a covariance matrix and its variance (the so-called step-size). Each update is based on the correlations observed in successful mutations. This allows CMA-ES to adapt its step-size and search directions (the covariance matrix) to the problem landscape. Despite its o⁡(d2)o(d^{2}) computational cost and memory usage, due the the handling of the full covariance matrix, it is widely regarded as a powerful and reliable optimizer.
D-CMA Ros and Hansen [2008] is the most popular of the several “tricks” that have been proposed to cope with this complexity. D-CMA uses a diagonal covariance matrix rather than a full positive definite matrix. Its efficiency, hence, depends on the degree of correlation between the variables, aka the separability of the objective function.
When handling a full population (μ>1\mu>1), both CMA-ES and D-CMA apply the adaptive Gaussian mutation to a linear recombination of the μ\mu individuals. The historical CMA-ES used the mean (all weights of the linear recombination are 1/μ1/\mu), whereas the state-of-the-art CMA-ES uses weights that decrease with the rank of each individual. In the latter case, more information is used, and the branching factor increases (see Sec. E.5).

As noted in Sec. 3.2, the simplest ESs (or EAs) are the (1+1)-EAs: the single current individual is modified, and the best of both becomes the new current one. While the already-mentioned OneFifth was the first historical successful adaptive EA (see again Alg. 2-Left), another family of (1+1)-EAs is directly derived from the historical GAs (Genetic Algorithms), that optimize bitstrings: the mutation typically flips each bit with a given probability. In the continuous case, the bitflip is turned into a “Gaussian flip”: each value is replaced by a value sampled from a standard normal mutation (𝒩⁡(0,1){\cal N}(0,1) in Alg. 2). Several variants of such “discrete-inspired” algorithms exist in Nevergrad, depending on the probability of applying this Gaussian flip to each variable. The Discrete algorithm exactly mimics the standard setting in GAs by adopting a fixed 1/d1/d probability; the Lengler Doerr et al. [2019], Einarsson et al. [2019] algorithm uses a gradually decreasing schedule. The Uniform-Disc Dang and Lehre [2016] algorithm uses a probability that is uniformly sampled in ]0,1]]0,1], and the FastGA Doerr et al. [2017] uses an α/d\alpha/d probability where α\alpha is sampled from a power-law distribution.
Additionally, COLengler is a variant of Lengler that also performs, after mutation, a coordinate-wise crossover à la differential evolution.

DE (Differential Evolution) Storn and Price [1997] evolves a population of individuals: each individual is mutated using (i) differences between good points (for taking into account the key directions) and, in its “Curr-to-best” variants (ii) typical differences between the population and the best point so far, before a coordinate-wise crossover is applied. In spite of its very low computational cost, DE is known as a very efficient algorithm.

PSO (Particle Swarm Optimization) Kennedy and Eberhart [1995] uses a population of moving individuals ("particles"), each with an associated velocity. At each iteration, the velocity of each particle is biased towards the best value observed so far by this particle, and towards the best value over the complete population of particles, and the particle moves according to its new velocity.

Furthermore, Nevergrad also includes some ensemble approaches.
NgIohTuned is a wizard. It chooses one algorithm from its portfolio of BBO algorithms, based on some characteristics of the problem, and following a hand-made rule. Portfolios and wizards have been first proposed for SAT solving [Xu et al., 2008], and later ported to black-box optimization [Awad et al., 2020, Meunier et al., 2021].
Bet-And-Run algorithms, for budget bb, consists in running kk algorithms with budget α​b/k\alpha b/k, picking up the one reaching the best objective value and running it for the remaining (1−α)​b(1-\alpha)b budget; 3-OneFifth is an instance of Bet-And-Run with α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and three OneFifth in parallel; with α=1\alpha=1, 3-Disc runs three Discrete in parallel and 2-DE/D-CMA runs DE and D-CMA.

These algorithms were chosen because of their finite branching factor: Tab. 3 lists the branching factors of all cited algorithms. As noted in Sec. 3.2, the branching factor is 2 for all (1+1) algorithms. The derivation of the other values is detailed in App. E.

Discussion. The choice of a BBO algorithm for a given problem is a long-lasting problem, and can of course be left to the Nevergrad wizard NgIohTuned. However, some characteristics of the algorithm introduced above are worth highlighting here, and might in turn give some information about the problems addressed with BBoxER based on its experimental results.
The adaptive approaches are now well mastered: CMA-ES offers the most sophisticated update mechanism. It is competitive in terms of performance with the best algorithms of Mathematical Programming, and has recently been proven to converge linearly Gissler [2024] However, it has a high computational complexity with respect to dimension dd and hence poorly scales up. Among several variants, D-CMA offers a very good compromise. But the simplest adaptive mechanism is that of OneFifth, which is very robust and often very efficient. Note, however, that its adaptation mechanism requires a number of iterations to take place, and was, for example, discarded in the OpenAI ES, one of the rare examples of large-scale BBO in complete training of Deep Neural Networks Salimans et al. [2017].
Because D-CMA only adapts a diagonal covariance matrix, one cannot expect that it effectively handles non-separable objectives. Less intuitively, this is also true for PSO, and, to a lesser extent, for DE unless its crossover rate is small Auger et al. [2009]. On the other hand, their adaptive mechanism (implicit for DE) makes CMA-ES, D-CMA and (some variants of) DE very efficient in dealing with randomly rotated ill-conditioned problems, which is not the case for PSO Auger et al. [2009].
Regarding the discrete-inspired (1+1)-EAs, Discrete, Uniform-Disc, Lengler, and FastGA, they are based on proved convergence proofs for known benchmark functions in the bitstring case, but their efficiency in the continuous setting is more surprising, and would deserve deep mathematical analyses.
Last but not least, Bet-And-Run algorithms, including 3-OneFifth, 3-Disc, and 2-DE/D-CMA, are robust, as proved in Sec. E.4 and demonstrated in the experimental results (Sec. 5 and App. I. However, they still require the choice of the embedded algorithms.

D.2 Possible Extensions

Code and Package. As said, all experiments in this work have been run on the Nevergrad open source platform Rapin and Teytaud [2018], which encompasses many BBO algorithms, along with specialized wizards that select among them based on problem-specific properties. Nevergrad also includes algorithms that are black-box optimizers without being comparison-based, such as [Powell, 1994, Powell, 1964]. Since these operate with a finite number of bits per loss function, they might also fall under the theoretical framework of Sec. 4, though this is left for future work.

Extension to multi-objective algorithms is another promising direction, for instance by optimizing different criteria (e.g., pass@k and accuracy) or by considering performance across several distinct benchmarks as the training objective, rather than averaging them.

Beyond Comparison-based Algorithms

An important assumption (5) is that the only thing that depends on the dataset DD is c​h​o​i​c​e1,…,c​h​o​i​c​ebchoice_{1},\dots,choice_{b}, and each c​h​o​i​c​eichoice_{i} has at most kik_{i} possible values (ki:=a​l​g.n​u​m​C​a​l​l​s​()k_{i}:=alg.numCalls() is called the branching factor Fournier and Teytaud [2011]). This is unusual in deep learning (DL), as in DL c​o​m​p​a​r​ecompare is replaced by some function involving gradients (even Reinforce Williams [1992a] or GRPO Shao et al. [2024] return a gradient update), and c​h​o​i​c​eichoice_{i} is replaced by a gradient, or, for reinforcement learning such as GRPO Shao et al. [2024], the outputs and their rewards.

Algorithms that do not return any gradient are termed black-box optimization algorithms. Among black-box optimization algorithms, some methods are comparison-based: they have finite kik_{i}. These comparison-based algorithms are typically classified in three families of algorithms:

(i) random search and derandomized variants McKay et al. [1979], Niederreiter [1992], (ii) direct search methods Roberts and Royer [2023], and (iii) evolutionary computation Beyer [2001]

. Note that GRPO Shao et al. [2024] is sometimes considered as gradient-free in the sense that it does not require the gradient of the loss function; however, it does require other detailed information about the outputs of models, so that it is not black-box in the same sense (and a fortiori not comparison-based), and the present results do not apply to GRPO or REINFORCE Williams [1992b] if we assume that they work on infinite-precision floats.

Taking into account the Finite Float Precision.

Because our results are mainly useful when kik_{i} is small, this work focused on comparison-based algorithms. However, all results of Sec. 4 are true for large values of kik_{i}. Let us check kik_{i} in the case of some classical methods for post-training. In BBoxER, the information flow from the data to the model is limited to roughly one bit per iteration, leading to at most 2b2^{b} possible outputs for a budget of bb steps. This limited capacity directly reflects the compression properties showcased in eq. 3 and fig. 2. In contrast, supervised fine-tuning updates the model using one gradient per mini-batch. For an 8B model with 16-bit precision, each mini-batch carries about 256B bits: a few mini-batches are sufficient to encode the entire content of Wikipedia. Reinforcement learning methods, such as GRPO, typically rely on model outputs and reward signals that would allow them to encode the full dataset within a single training epoch.

Appendix E Overfitting Bounds and their Generalizations

In this Section we provide the theoretical generalization bounds for the deterministic (Sec. E.1) and randomized cases (Sec. E.2), followed by (Sec. E.3) strengthened bounds for the special cases of (1,λ)(1,\lambda) and (1+λ)(1+\lambda) BBO algorithms as described in App. D. We proceed by making our bounds explicit for various families of algorithms, based on Fournier and Teytaud [2011]; in Sec. E.4 we obtain strengthened bounds for Bet-and-Run combinations like 3-OneFifth, MultiDisc, or 2-DE/D-CMA (deployed in some of our experiments in Sec. 5), Sec. E.5 lays out bounds for population-based evolution strategies (i.e., (μ+λ)(\mu+\lambda) and (μ,λ)(\mu,\lambda) with μ>1\mu>1) like CMA-ES and D-CMA, and Sec. E.6 deals with differential evolution and particle swarm optimization. The key to our results is the branching factor kik_{i}, i.e., the number of distinct behaviors of the algorithm that can arise in an iteration. Finally, Sec. E.7 derives explicit bounds as a function of the dataset size.

E.1 Bounds for the Deterministic Algorithm: Theorem 1

Theorem 1 (Deterministic case).

Let aa be an algorithm, bb a budget, ss the dataset size, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Assume N⁡(ω,a,b)N(\omega,a,b) is finite and that for some δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon}, ∀x,PωD​(|L^​(x)−L⁡(x)|>ϵ)≤δ1,ϵ.\forall x,\;P_{\omega_{D}}\left(|\widehat{L}(x)-L(x)|>\epsilon\right)\leq\delta_{1,\epsilon}. Then

PωD​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ)\displaystyle P_{\omega_{D}}\left(|\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon\right) ≤N⁡(ω,a,b)⋅δ1,ϵ.\displaystyle\leq N(\omega,a,b)\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}. (A.4)
PωD​(sup1≤i≤b|L^​(xi)−L⁡(xi)|≥ϵ)\displaystyle P_{\omega_{D}}\left(\sup_{1\leq i\leq b}|\widehat{L}(x_{i})-L(x_{i})|\geq\epsilon\right) ≤b⋅N⁡(ω,a,b)⋅δ1,ϵ.\displaystyle\leq b\cdot N(\omega,a,b)\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}. (A.5)
Proof.

For eq. A.4: apply the Bonferroni bound (eq. A.3) to the set of events

{|L^​(F​i​n​a​l​M​o​d​e​lω,D,a,b)−L⁡(F​i​n​a​l​M​o​d​e​lω,D,a,b)|>ϵ;D∈𝒟}.\{|\hat{L}(FinalModel_{\omega,D,a,b})-L(FinalModel_{\omega,D,a,b})|>\epsilon;D\in{\cal D}\}.

This set has cardinality at most N⁡(ω,a,b)N(\omega,a,b).

For eq. A.5, apply the Bonferroni bound to the set of events

{|L^​(m​o​d​e​lω,D,a,b,i)−L⁡(m​o​d​e​lω,D,a,b,i)|>ϵ;i∈{1,…,b},D∈𝒟},\{|\hat{L}(model_{\omega,D,a,b,i})-L(model_{\omega,D,a,b,i})|>\epsilon;i\in\{1,\dots,b\},D\in{\cal D}\},

where m​o​d​e​lω,D,a,b,imodel_{\omega,D,a,b,i} is mim_{i} when BBoxERis applied with seed ω\omega, algorithm aa, budget bb, dataset DD. This set has cardinality b⋅N⁡(ω,a,b)b\cdot N(\omega,a,b). ∎

E.2 Generalization Bounds for Randomized BBoxER

Thm 1 applies to deterministic algorithms, where the only source of randomness is the sampling of the dataset DD, determined by the seed ωD\omega_{D}. In this case, the deviation risk δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon} is computed over that randomness alone. When the optimization algorithm itself is randomized (i.e., ω\omega is a random seed), the deviation risk δϵ,ω\delta_{\epsilon,\omega} also depends on ω\omega. Averaging over ω\omega yields the total deviation risk:

δϵ=𝔼ω​δϵ,ω.\delta_{\epsilon}=\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\delta_{\epsilon,\omega}.

Since the bound of Thm 1 holds uniformly for any fixed ω\omega, it extends naturally to the randomized setting, in which x^\widehat{x} depends on both ω\omega and ωD\omega_{D}:

Theorem 3 (Stochastic case).

Consider a randomized seed ω\omega (i.e. ω\omega is a random variable), an algorithm aa and a budget b∈ℕb\in{\mathbb{N}}. Then

OPENPω,ωD​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ))≤(supω​ constantN⁡(ω,a,b))⋅δ1,ϵ.P_{\omega,\omega_{D}}(|\hat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon))\leq\left(\sup_{\omega\mbox{ constant}}N(\omega,a,b)\right)\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}.

Here, the probability is taken over both ω\omega (which determines the optimization trajectory and hence the final model x^\widehat{x}) and ωD\omega_{D} (which governs dataset sampling). The supremum is over a constant ω\omega, and x^\widehat{x} can be built with a random variable ω\omega.

Application to Random Search.

In this case, the bb candidate models are sampled independently of the data. Since each choice is fixed a priori, the number of internal states satisfies N⁡(ω,random-search,b)≤bN(\omega,\texttt{random-search},b)\leq b. N⁡(ω,a,b)N(\omega,a,b) is derived from kb=bk_{b}=b (we choose between the bb models x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} at the very end) and ki=1k_{i}=1 for other values of ii. Apply the Bonferroni correction to the N⁡(ω,a,b)N(\omega,a,b) possible values of x^\widehat{x} leads to

PωD​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ)≤b⋅δ1,ϵ.P_{\omega_{D}}(|\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon)\leq b\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}\ . (A.6)

This also applies to quasi-random strategies and design of experiments, where the sampling of hyperparameters does not depend on their empirical performance. In these cases, we observe that bb can be exponential in ss without overfitting.

E.3 Comparison-based Strategies: the (1,λ)(1,\lambda) and (1+λ)(1+\lambda) Cases.

In contrast to random search, where all candidate parametrizations are chosen independently of their evaluation, comparison-based algorithms build candidates iteratively based on performance. If λ\lambda candidates are evaluated at each step and the best is retained, then the number of internal states after one iteration is λ\lambda; after two iterations, λ2\lambda^{2}; and after n=b/λn=b/\lambda iterations, at most λn\lambda^{n}. The total risk is, therefore, bounded by λn⋅δ1,ϵ\lambda^{n}\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}, where nn is the number of iterations with ki>1k_{i}>1 (with ki=λk_{i}=\lambda in such iterations); see Fournier and Teytaud [2011].

In the elitist variant (1+λ)(1+\lambda), the best model is selected among the current best and the λ\lambda new candidates, so ki∈{1,λ+1}k_{i}\in\{1,\lambda+1\}. This leads to a total number of internal states bounded by (λ+1)(b−1)/λ(\lambda+1)^{(b-1)/\lambda}. Simply apply Thm 3 in the case

  • •

    ki=λk_{i}=\lambda if i+1​ mod ​λ=0i+1\mbox{ mod }\lambda=0 (every λt​h\lambda^{th} iterations we pick up the best of the previous λ\lambda models).

  • •

    ki=1k_{i}=1 otherwise.

and the corresponding generalization bound becomes:

P⁡(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ)≤(λ+1)(b−1)/λ⋅δ1,ϵ.P(|\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon)\leq(\lambda+1)^{(b-1)/\lambda}\cdot\delta_{1,\epsilon}\ . (A.7)

For example, this applies to the (1+1)(1+1) evolution strategy with the one-fifth success rule or the Lengler variant Einarsson et al. [2019], both corresponding to ki=2k_{i}=2.

E.4 Generalization Bounds for Bet-And-Run Combinations

Consider the example in eq. A.7. Additionally, if we perform k>1k>1 independent optimization runs, and if the budget bb is divided by kk, then the Bonferroni correction leads to a risk

k⏟Bonferroni correction⋅λ(b/(λ⋅k))⏟Branching factor per run⋅δ1,ϵ⏟Risk for a single model\underbrace{k}_{\text{Bonferroni correction}}\cdot\underbrace{\lambda^{(b/(\lambda\cdot k))}}_{\text{Branching factor per run}}\cdot\underbrace{\delta_{1,\epsilon}}_{\text{Risk for a single model}} (A.8)

for the resulting parametrization. According to these bounds, increasing the number kk of independent runs for a given total budget decreases the risk of overfitting. More generally, consider b​e​t−a​n​d−r​u​n​(a1,a2,…,ak)bet-and-run(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}), the bet-and-run of kk algorithms a1a_{1},…,aka_{k}. This algorithm, for a budget bb, runs each aia_{i} with budget b/kb/k:

  • •

    These kk runs are completely independent.

  • •

    Its random seed is split into kk random seeds ω1,…,ωk\omega^{1},\dots,\omega^{k}.

  • •

    At the end, we choose the model with best empirical performance, i.e. x^\widehat{x} is x^i=F​i​n​a​l​M​o​d​e​l​(ωi,ai,b/k)\widehat{x}_{i}=FinalModel(\omega^{i},a_{i},b/k) minimizing L^​(x^i)\hat{L}(\widehat{x}_{i}).

Theorem 4 (Bet and Run has low overfitting risk).

Consider b​e​t−a​n​d−r​u​n​(a1,a2,…,ak)bet-and-run(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}).Then

N⁡(ω,b​e​t−a​n​d−r​u​n​(a1,a2,…,ak),b)≤∑i=1kN⁡(ω,ai,b/k).N(\omega,bet-and-run(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}),b)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}N(\omega,a_{i},b/k). (A.9)
Proof.

The final outcome x^\widehat{x} is one of the x^i\widehat{x}_{i}, so the number of possible outcomes is the sum of the numbers of possible outcomes of each algorithm individually. ∎

Let us consider that the aia_{i} are all the same algorithm, and let us check the impact of bet-and-run on overfitting. eq. A.9 implies a lower overfitting than with a single algorithm (corresponding to N⁡(ω,ai,b)N(\omega,a_{i},b)) if N⁡(ω,ai,b/k)N(\omega,a_{i},b/k) increases more than linearly in b/kb/k, which is the case for most optimization algorithms. For example, with (1+1)(1+1) evolution strategies, Sec. E.3 shows that N⁡(ω,e​v​o​l​u​t​i​o​n​_​s​t​r​a​t​e​g​y,b)N(\omega,evolution\_strategy,b) is exponential in bb.

Let us illustrate this in an example. Consider eq. 5 in the case ki≤2k_{i}\leq 2, namely:

PωD​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ)≤2⋅exp⁡(ln⁡2⋅b−2​s​ϵ2).P_{\omega_{D}}\left(|\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon\right)\leq 2\cdot\exp(\ln 2\cdot b-2s\epsilon^{2}).

With a bet-and-run of 33 algorithms, it becomes:

PωD​(|L^​(x^)−L⁡(x^)|≥ϵ)≤2⋅exp⁡(ln⁡2⋅(log2⁡(3)+b/3)−2​s​ϵ2).P_{\omega_{D}}\left(|\widehat{L}(\widehat{x})-L(\widehat{x})|\geq\epsilon\right)\leq 2\cdot\exp(\ln 2\cdot(\log_{2}(3)+b/3)-2s\epsilon^{2}). (A.10)

which is better (lower) as b→∞b\to\infty.

E.5 Population-Based Evolution Strategies (e.g. CMA-ES and D-CMA)

For a (μ+1)(\mu+1) evolution strategy which stores a full ranking of the population of size μ\mu, each new point has (1+μ)(1+\mu) possible ranks: from best to worst in a list of cardinal 1+μ1+\mu, so the bound becomes (1+μ)N−μ(1+\mu)^{N-\mu}. Extensions are possible for (μ,λ)(\mu,\lambda) or (μ+λ)(\mu+\lambda) evolution strategies:

N⁡(ω,(μ,λ),a=(μ,λ)​-ES,b)\displaystyle N(\omega,(\mu,\lambda),a=(\mu,\lambda)\mbox{-ES},b) ≤\displaystyle\leq (λμ)b−μλ\displaystyle{\binom{\lambda}{\mu}}^{\frac{b-\mu}{\lambda}}
N⁡(ω,(μ+λ),a=(μ+λ)​-ES,b)\displaystyle N(\omega,(\mu+\lambda),a=(\mu+\lambda)\mbox{-ES},b) ≤\displaystyle\leq (λ+μμ)b−μλ\displaystyle{\binom{\lambda+\mu}{\mu}}^{\frac{b-\mu}{\lambda}}

In the case of CMA or D-CMA, the (μ,λ)(\mu,\lambda) strategy is more usual and used in our experiments; and typically, the population-size λ\lambda is set as λ=4+⌊3​log⁡(d)⌋\lambda=4+\lfloor 3\log(d)\rfloor in dimension dd, and μ\mu frequently scales as λ/4\lambda/4 or λ/2\lambda/2. Sometimes there is a complete ranking of the μ\mu selected points so that different weights are used for the μ\mu selected points depending on their rank: this adds a factor μ!\mu! to the number of possible branches: otherwise, we get bounds as in Tab. 3.

E.6 Differential Evolution (DE) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)

For differential evolution without storing the best so far, each point is just compared to its parent: we get 2b​δ1,ϵ2^{b}\delta_{1,\epsilon}: this suggests that recombination is not a problem as it does not increase the number of bits of information. When the best so far is stored, we have 3 possibilities: worse than parent, better than parent but not better than best so far, and new best so far: so the bound is 3b​δ1,ϵ3^{b}\delta_{1,\epsilon}. Similar bounds are straightforward for PSO.

E.7 Dependence on Dataset Size: Scaling and Numerical Application

Sec. C.2 presents classical large deviation inequalities, and the present paper shows how, in the case of comparison-based algorithms, we can derive non-vacuous bounds. Let us now see numerically how our overfitting bound behaves in practical cases.

We have focused on bounds (on the generalization loss of the model obtained by optimization) derived from a given δ1,ϵ\delta_{1,\epsilon} (obtained for a single model):

We have seen in eq. A.2 that, using Hoeffding’s bound, δ1,ϵ=2​exp⁡(−2​s​ϵ2)\delta_{1,\epsilon}=2\exp(-2s\epsilon^{2}) with s=|D|s=|D| the sample size, and δ≤2×(2b)​exp⁡(−s​ϵ2)\delta\leq 2\times(2^{b})\exp(-s\epsilon^{2}), leading to δ\delta constant when bb scales linearly with ss: the acceptable number of iterations (i.e., a fixed bound on δ\delta) is linear in the sample size DD. Applying Hoeffding, and aiming at a risk δ\delta, we get that overfitting at level ϵ\epsilon is impossible if

b≤ln⁡(δ)+2​s​ϵ2ln⁡(2)−1.b\leq\frac{\ln(\delta)+2s\epsilon^{2}}{\ln(2)}-1.

If we prefer the Bennet&Bernstein inequality (based on an assumption on the standard deviation, see Sec. C.1 [Devroye et al., 1996, Section 8.2]), we get

b≤s​ϵ​h1​(ϵ/σ2)ln⁡(2)+ln⁡(δ)ln⁡(2)−1.b\leq{\frac{s\epsilon h_{1}(\epsilon/\sigma^{2})}{\ln(2)}}+\frac{\ln(\delta)}{\ln(2)}-1.

This equation, for s=8000s=8000 examples (close to GSM8k), δ=12\delta=\frac{1}{2} (we are considering the median case), ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01 (we want that precision) and σ=0.06\sigma=0.06 (the standard variation of the loss is 0.06, we assume that the initial model is already good), leads to the claim that a budget b≤91b\leq 91 cannot lead to overfitting. If we assume ϵ=0.04\epsilon=0.04 and σ=0.3\sigma=0.3, we get with Hoeffding a bound 3434 and with Bennet&Bernstein a bound 8888. With ϵ=0.06\epsilon=0.06, σ=0.3\sigma=0.3, Bennet&Bernstein leads to a budget 189189. The budget becomes 482482 if we use ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1, σ=0.3\sigma=0.3. Also, these bounds scale linearly with the number ss of feedbacks (dataset size or number of feedbacks in A/B testings). These numbers are low, but we see that bounds are not vacuous even in realistic scenarios.

Appendix F Consequences for Privacy and Poisoning

F.1 Privacy by Design

In the context of large language models, privacy typically refers to users’ desire to prevent their inputs, such as queries or conversations, from being inferred or reconstructed. Several studies have shown that gradient-based training methods can leak such information Zhu et al. [2019], Hitaj et al. [2017], Haim et al. [2022], Carlini et al. [2021].

In contrast, the BBoxER approach is an instance of privacy by design Gershoff [2025]: It does not rely on gradients, nor does it require access to the raw content of user sessions. Instead, it only leverages a binary satisfaction signal–whether a user prefers one version of the model over another. This can be collected via simple A/B testing, and the algorithm proceeds using aggregated comparison outcomes. In particular, our method operates without knowledge of the specific queries or model responses, which never leave the user’s device.

BBoxER privacy guarantees can be framed in terms of differential privacy Dwork [2008], which ensures that the output of a training algorithm does not change significantly when a single data point is modified. Given two datasets D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} differing by a single element, differential privacy requires that for any output set SS,

P⁡(A⁡(D1)∈S)≤exp⁡(ϵ)⋅P⁡(A⁡(D2)∈S)+δ.P(A(D_{1})\in S)\leq\exp(\epsilon)\cdot P(A(D_{2})\in S)+\delta. (A.11)

We now examine how this applies in two distinct cases: the privacy of user queries and responses and the privacy of satisfaction feedback.

Privacy of Queries and Responses.

Our algorithm never observes the actual content of user interactions. If D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} differ by one prompt or answer or any data unrelated to preference signals, then the outcome of Alg. 1 remains unchanged. In that case, the algorithm behaves identically on both datasets, satisfying differential privacy with ϵ=0\epsilon=0, δ=0\delta=0. This guarantee is stronger than what is typically offered in federated learning: since no gradients are shared or aggregated, the system is inherently robust to inference attacks such as those in Zhu et al. [2019], Hitaj et al. [2017], Carlini et al. [2021].

Privacy of Satisfaction Signals.

We may also be interested in the privacy implications of modifying a single satisfaction response rir_{i} associated with a specific user. While this is less sensitive than access to the user’s actual queries or responses, it still reflects individual feedback and may warrant protection. In this setting, we consider the case where D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} differ by exactly one such response, altered during a run.

Applying eq. 6 with k=1k=1, we get that A⁡(D1)A(D_{1}) and A⁡(D2)A(D_{2}) are the same with probability at least 1−3​b/2​n​π1-3b/\sqrt{2n\pi} when we have nn data points and bb iterations. This corresponds to differential privacy with ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and δ=3​b/2​n​π\delta=3b/\sqrt{2n\pi}.

Comparison with Other Approaches.

In supervised fine-tuning, both inputs and outputs are required for training. Reinforcement learning additionally requires access to the model’s responses and reward signals. While federated learning aims to limit privacy leakage by aggregating gradients locally, it still exposes sensitive intermediate data—such as gradients—that have been shown to be vulnerable to attacks Hitaj et al. [2017]. In contrast, our approach bypasses these vulnerabilities entirely by never interacting with such information in the first place.

F.2 Poisoning

Poisoning attacks seek to influence the outcome of a learning algorithm by injecting malicious data. This threat has been widely studied in machine learning Biggio et al. [2012], Pathmanathan et al. [2025], Wan et al. [2023b], and it is particularly relevant in interactive settings such as retrofitting. In our context, a poisoning attempt manipulates up to kk user feedbacks per iteration to bias the optimization process.

Our robustness Thm 2 quantifies the impact of such attacks: the probability that the final model is altered remains bounded by (2​k+1)​b2​n​π\frac{(2k+1)b}{\sqrt{2n\pi}}. This implies that an adversary must control k∼n/bk\sim\sqrt{n}/b feedbacks per round to affect the result significantly. Such an attack becomes increasingly difficult as the number of users nn grows.

Importantly, this guarantee holds even under a strong adversarial model Kearns and Li [1993], where the attacker is computationally unbounded and has full knowledge of the system. In practice, this highlights the resilience of our retrofitting method to small-scale poisoning.

G.2 Theorem on Data Extraction and Proof of Corollary 2

corollary 2 is a direct consequence of the following Theorem.

Theorem 5.

The cardinality of the set of possible outputs of BBoxER for a given m0,ω,a,bm_{0},\omega,a,b is bounded as follows:

#⁡{BBoxER​(m0,ω,Di,a,b);i∈{1,…,n}}≤supD∏i=1bki.\#\{\mbox{{BBoxER}{}}(m_{0},\omega,D_{i},a,b);i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}\leq\sup_{D}\prod_{i=1}^{b}k_{i}. (A.14)
Proof.

eq. A.14 is an immediate consequence of eq. 1.

If A⁡(m0,D):=A(m_{0},D):=BBoxER (m0,ω,D,a,b)(m_{0},\omega,D,a,b), then vulnerability to data extraction as in eq. 7 immediately implies that {E⁡(A⁡(m0,Di));i∈{1,…,n}}\{E(A(m_{0},D_{i}));i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\} has cardinal at least nn, and therefore {A⁡(m0,Di);i∈{1,…,n}}\{A(m_{0},D_{i});i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\} has cardinal at least nn. If 2b>n2^{b}>n and ki≤2k_{i}\leq 2, this contradicts eq. A.14.

∎

This means that no matter how large ss is, retrofitting can only produce a number of different outputs upper-bounded by the product over the kik_{i}, which represent the number of possible data-dependent choices per iteration - e.g., 2b2^{b} for algorithms with ki≤2k_{i}\leq 2 and bb iterations.

Appendix H Experimental Details

Here we provide details for the settings of the experiments in Sec. 5. The licenses for all datasets used in this work can be found in Tab. 4.

All BBO algorithms are used with their default parameters in Nevergrad [Rapin and Teytaud, 2018]. At each iteration of Alg. 1, the modified model is evaluated on GSM8k train (8-shot, unless otherwise specified) and the objective function to optimize is the exact match. At the end of each run, the FinalModel is evaluated on the same objective function. Specifically, we compute the performance of m​o​d​i​f​i​e​d​(m0,x^)modified(m_{0},\hat{x}) where x^\hat{x} is the update that reaches the best objective function value during training.

Experiment 1.

We apply BBoxER (Alg. 1) with rank-1 (LoRA) multiplicative parameter updates on the unembedding layer, as detailed in App. B. In both base and instruct models, the total number of parameters to optimize is h​i​d​d​e​n​_​d​i​m+v​o​c​a​b​_​s​i​z​e=4096+128,256=132,352hidden\_dim+vocab\_size=4096+128,256=132,352. Each iteration requires 2min30s on 32 A100 GPUs.

Experiment 2.

We explore 3 setups on Llama3.1-8B:

  • 1.

    First attention layer, where we perform a broadcast multiplicative update to the Q matrix in the first attention layer by broadcasting a vector of size 40964096 to the 4096×40964096\times 4096 Q matrix and then using the update formula as in Sec. B.1.

  • 2.

    All attention layers, where we perform a broadcast multiplicative update on all the QQ matrices of all attention layers. Resulting in n​_​l​a​y​e​r​s×h​i​d​d​e​n​_​d​i​m=32×4096=131,072n\_layers\times hidden\_dim=32\times 4096=131,072 parameters to optimize, using the update formula as in Sec. B.2

  • 3.

    All attention layers and no few-shot, where we apply a broadcast multiplicative update on all the QQ matrices of all attention layers, as in 2 above. However, we do not include any few-shot examples in the prompt during either training or testing.

All experiments are carried out with budget b=150b=150 unless otherwise specified. In addition to GSM8k test, we also evaluate the results on GSM+ (8-shot) and SVAMP (8-shot). Each iteration requires 2min30s on 32 A100 GPUs.

Experiment 3

In this experiment, D-CMA is used to directly optimize all normalization layers of Llama3.1-8B(-Instruct) and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (without using any low rank modification). The number of updated parameters is n​_​n​o​r​m​_​l​a​y​e​r​s×h​i​d​d​e​n​_​d​i​m=65×4096=266,240n\_norm\_layers\times hidden\_dim=65\times 4096=266,240 for Llama3.1-8B(-Instruct) and n​_​n​o​r​m​_​l​a​y​e​r​s×h​i​d​d​e​n​_​d​i​m=73×2048=149,504n\_norm\_layers\times hidden\_dim=73\times 2048=149,504 for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. All experiments are conducted with budget b∈{150,300}b\in\{150,300\}. Furthermore, we evaluate on additional mathematical reasoning benchmarks: MATH500 (4-shot), Hellaswag (0-shot), GSM+ test_mini (8-shot), ARC Easy (0-shot) and ARC Challenge (0-shot), AMC23 (0-shot). Each iteration requires 2min30s on 32 A100 GPUs for Llama3.1-8B(-Instruct) and 3min on 24 A100 GPUs for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.

Appendix I Additional Experiments

In this section, we describe extensions of the experiments performed in Sec. 5, in particular for Bet-and-Run variants and for training on larger datasets.

Extensions of Experiment 2.

We have performed additional experiments on Llama3.1-8B in the spirit of Experiment 2 (Sec. 5), by modifying the output layer instead of the attention layers, using a multiplicative update by broadcasting a vector of size v​o​c​a​b​_​s​i​z​e=128,256vocab\_size=128,256 as described in Sec. B.1. We also experiment with two different update constants in {0.01,0.0001}\{0.01,0.0001\}. Tab. 5 shows the results. We see improvements particularly for the larger update constant and Bet-and-Run algorithms.

Experiment 3 for Bet-and-Run Algorithms.

The theoretical results in Sec. E.4 demonstrate that Bet-and-Run algorithms enable the use of larger budgets without risks of overfitting. This has been partially validated in Experiment 2 by the results of 3-OneFifth, performing well even with greater budget (Table 1). We here extend this analysis and report Bet-and-Run results for the setup of Experiment 3 in Tab. 6. Specifically, we run BBoxER under the same setup as in Experiment 3 (detailed in App. H), and use the BetAndRun (N, b) variant of D-CMA, where we run D-CMA for N different runs with budget b′=N/bb^{\prime}=N/b, and pick the update x^\hat{x} that performed the best across these runs. In practice, we use the runs with 5 different seeds from Tab. 2 and report the mean and standard deviation of all possible combinations (5N)\binom{5}{N} with N∈{3,4}N\in\{3,4\}.

Comparing the results in Tab. 6 with those in Tab. 2 (BBoxER without Bet-and-Run), we observe that in 100% runs (with or without Bet-and-Run) BBoxER improves results; in 83% of cases Bet-and-Run outperforms its base counterpart.

Experiment 3 for Larger Training Sets.

In Tab. 7 we report the results of running BBoxER with a larger training dataset. This experiment is motivated by the theoretical prediction that the allowable budget scales linearly with the dataset size. Formally, we adopt the same experimental setup as in Experiment 3 (see App. H), but in addition to GSM8k train (7,473 samples), we also include the MATH train set (7500 samples) into the training set, thus doubling its size compared to previous experiments. We define the objective function for BBoxER to be the average of exact matches (EM) across both datasets : m​e​t​r​i​c=12​E​M​(G​S​M​8​k)+12​E​M​(M​A​T​H)metric=\frac{1}{2}EM(GSM8k)+\frac{1}{2}EM(MATH). We run BBoxER with a budget of up to b=1200b=1200 and evaluate the model every 150 iterations. As the budget increases, we observe eventual overfitting. Interestingly, we find that the Llama3.1-8B base model does not overfit on the GSM8k test set and continues to improve, contrary to its instruct variant, which begins to overfit earlier. See also fig. 3 for illustration of performance gain on some of the benchmarks.

Further Discussion of all Experiments.

Consistent with our theoretical results, our results are robust and show performance improvement with little to no overfitting even with larger budgets. We note that even when running various experiments with randomly chosen parameters, significant performance drops are rare: In fig. 1 and in Tab. 1, all data points are independent from one another (i.e. computed independently); This allows us to compute P-values (App. J) to support our claims of statistical significance of the observed performance improvements.

In order to contextualize our findings, we can also compare to post-training with GRPO which proved to be highly effective on reasoning tasks. Most works deploy GRPO on larger training sets and we were unable to find results for the models deployed in our study. However, as shown in  Lin et al. [2025], GRPO achieved a notable 22% improvement when training a Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct model on the GSM8k dataset, leading to results between 77% and 81% with 1B models, without transfer to OOD. However, such improvement jumps tend to shrink with larger models. Nevertheless, though the Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct model we use already starts at nearly 80%, it is improved to 84% by BBoxER (Tab. 6).

There are only few works that train on GSM8k and study OOD transfer. The authors of  Sun et al. [2025a] employ an ’on-policy’ training approach, generating training samples through model prompting and subsequently fine-tuning on the resulting question-answer pairs. Their approach yields significant gains on both GSM8k and GSM+ benchmarks when evaluated in a zero-shot setting, by up to 28.8% on GSM8k with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct. However, the gains are less pronounced in the 5-shot setting, with an increase of 1.8% using self-consistency and 5 generations, figures that are close to those obtained by BBoxER on GSM8k and GSM+, as can be seen in Tab. 6.
In any case, remember that our goal in this work is not to achieve state-of-the-art performances on these and other benchmarks, but rather to show that our approach sacrifices little for provable privacy and overfitting guarantees.

Appendix J P-values

Contemporary papers on LLMs frequently involve a small number of experiments, due to the significant computational burden. But because we run independent tests, we can compute rigorous p-values by Fisher’s exact test, getting a measure of statistical significance despite the moderate number of experiments:

  • •

    We computed the pp-value of the frequency of green vs red in the columns of Tab. 1 and Tab. 5, the null hypothesis being "the probability of improvement is ≤0.5\leq 0.5".

  • •

    For the values in fig. 1, we computed the pp-value for the obtained frequency of successful runs (i.e., runs above baseline, vs below baseline) for budget >20>20, under the null hypothesis "the probability of improvement is ≤0.5\leq 0.5".

  • •

    In Experiment 3, we run BBoxER with budget b=150b=150 or b=300b=300. For each column of results we performed an exact Fisher test on all BBoxER runs (both 150 and 300, without considering the Bet-And-Runs) and computed p-values: there is therefore one pp-value per downstream task, against the null hypothesis "there is a probability of improvement ≤12\leq\frac{1}{2}". These different tests are not independent.

When computing p-values from tables of results, we used the initial data, not the averaged ones, obtaining one data point per independent run.

P-values Values.

Experiment 1: P-values in fig. 1 are 3​e−83e^{-8} (left), 3​e−53e^{-5} (right).

Experiment 2:

  • •

    Tab. 1: P-values are significant for GSM (5​e−35e^{-3}) and GSM+ (0.030.03), not for SVAMP.

  • •

    Tab. 5: P-values are 0.003 for GSM, 0.5 for the transfer to GSM+, no improvement for SVAMP.
